plan.title: Kindle vs Paper: Which Helps You Remember More?
plan.description: A quick look at what research says about reading on a Kindle versus paper books. Learn where paper wins on comprehension, where the two tie, and how to choose.

beats.narration: You may remember less from a Kindle than from a paper book. Scientists have tested this for twenty years, and the answer is not simple.
A 2018 meta-analysis combined 54 experiments. Its verdict: paper has a clear advantage for understanding what you read.

props.label: experiments combined in a 2018 meta-analysis, favoring paper

beats.narration: Researchers call it the screen inferiority effect. People often understand and remember less from digital text than from print.

props.definition: People often understand and remember less from digital texts than from print.

beats.narration: But a study of a long story found no difference on most measures between a Kindle and a pocket book. Even reading time matched.
Why might paper help? Scrolling, clicking and pop-ups can break the careful act of reading. A page gives more physical cues for building the story.
Readers still love print. Through the first nine months of 2026, US print unit sales were down just 0.1%.
So for study or deep reading, choose paper. For travel and casual reading, a Kindle is fine. Match the device to the job.

props.text: For learning, choose paper. For leisure, choose either.

mismatch_scenes: beat 5 (diagram): its narration never says ['Distraction', 'Weaker story schema']

accuracy.reason: The 54-experiment 2018 meta-analysis and the 0.1% print sales dip are traceable to the notes. But the diagram shows 'Scrolling and clicks' on a Kindle, which has no pop-ups, and the 'Weaker story schema' node is attached to a distraction chain the sources don't make. 'Tested for twenty years' is loosely supported.

coverage.reason: The script covers only comprehension. It skips portability, eye strain, battery, price, feel and the environmental angle, all of which the reviewer's note expects.

structure.reason: The order is clear: claim, meta-analysis, counter-study, why, then takeaway. The sales beat is a detour.

hook_ending.reason: The opening claim 'You may remember less from a Kindle' is decent. The ending is a generic 'Match the device to the job'.

tone.reason: Neutral, clear and suited to a general US audience.

visuals.reason: Scene types vary. The versus table has a truncated label ('Most comprehension measu') and an odd 'No difference' vs 'No difference' row. The diagram uses phone and cloud icons that fit poorly.

originality.reason: The 'screen inferiority effect' is a useful term, but the script is otherwise a generic research summary with no vivid example.

instructions.reason: It was asked for a short, fair comparison of Kindle and paper across practical factors. It delivers a narrow memory-research piece and misses most requested points. Length is about right.

language.reason: Fluent, clean sentences, with a slightly redundant repeat in beat 3.

defects.quote: Match the device to the job.

defects.issue: This is applied to Kindles, but the notes describe general digital text. E-readers rarely have pop-ups, so the claim is misleading.

The title narrows the brief to memory, whereas the request was a general comparison.
